title: can you guys share prompts to add for a 3d game development which significantly improves the way ai makes.
author: Best-Increase-1653
selftext:
Mine is running simulations in AI to find all the ways it can make mistakes or do bad things, then telling it to set these things as rules. After that, I make it work, and it works very, very well. However, it takes up a lot of tokens and time.

I am interested in learning more ways to make AI produce better results. also creating unique and different AI agents with detailed prompts that judge everything, and then the AI learns, sets up new rules, and works again. like how human wants every detail to be meaning full so i made ai do same also making ai think from all possibilities and doing everything i said in each possibility so it looks more like good game than ai slop. 

Another approach, which I believe is the most powerful, is making AI research and think very hard about how a true professional human thinks like finding the thought process of a very pro human and then ai think from that thought process.

I would love to learn more from all of you, because I am still a beginner.

comments.author: RyanStonepeak

comments.author: svdomer09
comments.body:
I don't think "better prompting" or prompt engineering is relevant as its own thing anymore. What's more important is having a good stack of agents, processes and documentation to make sure your vision is being translated and communicated properly. I would: 

• Research what the game development technical infrastructure works, so you can understand what AI is doing, why and how you can reposition it.   
• Make sure you have a conversation with the AI where you are sure it understands what you're trying to do before it starts coding.   
• If you're a beginner, don't try to dictate the technical solution, but rather talk to the AI about what result you want to achieve. 

I found with game development, telling the AI how I want something to \*feel\* is much more important and gives better results. For example, I am working on a racing game and I told the AI I wanted a section of track to "feel like riding through the forests of Endor like in the ROTJ scene" and it created something much better to start

replies.author: Vegetable_Voice_2044
replies.body:
A stack of agents? I've been relying on just Claude in a two week long conversation where I telm it what I want and give a reference to other games using that exact mechanic. And Claude writes it all up into a design document to follow when I finally permit it to create the content in my godot project. It seperates its tasks out into steps for implementation based on what the systems are and sets the dependant systems into the later steps (up to 28 steps so far)
 And I test the implementation of each step as we go. Only permitting one step to be implemented in a single "make stuff" prompt. Such as create a inventory user interface to these exact specifications, using this game or image as a reference.

How would multiple agents help my process? I also have run out of clear vision if what I want to do at this point and am brainstorming right into the prompts and asking the model for pushback based on what's commonly liked or disliked in games of the chosen genre or with relevant features and if it would conflict with the flow of gameplay.

replies.author: svdomer09
replies.body:
Well, for example for the game I'm working on I have:   
• A coordinator session that hands out work and tells me status  
• A track designer agent that is only focus on making track layouts   
• a scenery designer that dresses the tracks  
• character animation agent that only works on characters

that way they can also work in parallel and not have their context polluted by different requests

replies.author: InsolentCoolRadio
replies.body:
Gotcha lol

I’d strongly recommend looking into adding Tripo to your workflow

I saw all kinds of posts about people one-shotting beautiful 3D art with Astra or Fable, etc. and I blew weeks of compute across different agents having them pilot Blender and iterating on experiments to get slightly better than awful results

(Scaramanga is a wholly fictional character and there is no functional golden gun)

For additional context, in the times before AI I spent a few years training myself to make 2D art and I was focused on that, so 3D was a big deal to me, even with AI assistance

Anyway, I gave Tripo a model sheet of one of my characters, hit generate, and a few minutes later it spit out something exponentially better than what my LLM-based agents were able to do in Blender (at a cost of maybe $0.40)

There’s obviously way more to it than that, but if your boat is anything like mine was I think that would probably save a lot of your money, compute, time, and sanity

I haven’t tried Meshy, but people speak highly of it for AI-driven 3D work as well

comments.author: WhosLive
comments.body: Usually the biggest gain is shrinking each request instead of adding more prompt rules. Worth trying a short written spec of the game (core loop, controls, what done looks like), then asking for one small system at a time and testing it before moving on. Another thing that tends to help is keeping a running rules file with only the mistakes that actually happened, so it stays short and costs fewer tokens. Asking the AI to explain its plan back in plain words before coding also catches a lot of misunderstandings early.

comments.author: Vindelator
comments.body:
"Look at the images I've uploaded for color palette reverences." That's a bigger boon than it sounds.   
  
Upload images of nature too for references, not just other games. Want to add butterfly wings? In goes a pic of a butterfly. 

"Here's 5 references of cell shading i want applied to this."

Also, write all the UI and tooltips and dialogue by hand. I always have it include everything it's written for me in a text file that I fix myself. People don't think like machines so their instructions suck and are too long.
